questions.prompt: Why might a lower-contrast combination be kept intentionally?

options.text: Because the goal is to trick automated auditing tools.
Because constraints can conflict, such as a strict brand lock or intentional visual hierarchy.
Because high contrast drains too much battery life.

questions.explanation: Design involves tradeoffs; brand requirements or visual hierarchy may lead to a lower-contrast choice.
questions.hint: Consider what happens when a client will not alter their logo colors.
questions.testedLearningPoint: Recognize situations where strict contrast constraints conflict with brand rules.

questions.prompt: What is the primary benefit of documenting a tradeoff decision?

options.text: It automatically fixes the contrast ratio in the final code.
It creates transparency for developers and future audits, preventing confusion.
It legally protects the company from all accessibility lawsuits.
It hides the issue from automated scanning software permanently.

questions.explanation: Documentation shows that the issue was evaluated and a deliberate choice was made.
questions.hint: Think about what a developer needs to know when they see a failing color.
questions.testedLearningPoint: Record intentional design decisions for development teams.

questions.prompt: How does a documented tradeoff differ from a silent failure?

options.text: A silent failure means the contrast passes, while a tradeoff means it fails.
A silent failure causes confusion, while a tradeoff provides an acknowledged written justification.
A documented tradeoff is only used for text, while silent failures apply to images.
There is no difference between the two.

questions.explanation: Ignoring an issue leaves the team guessing, while a record explains why the color was kept.
questions.hint: It is about the difference between ignoring a problem and explaining it.
questions.testedLearningPoint: Differentiate between an ignored error and a documented tradeoff.
